newsitem.title: USA: Montgomery Ward case raises question - who's in charge.
newsitem.headline: Montgomery Ward case raises question - who's in charge.

text.p: Montgomery Ward & Co. Inc.'s bankruptcy case raises questions not only about the 125-year-old retailer's fate but also about who controls it, experts said Thursday.
The department store chain, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection Monday, is 58 percent-owned by General Electric Capital Services, a unit of General Electric Co.
GE Capital has wielded tremendous power over many facets of Montgomery Ward's business, which the retailer's lenders fear could affect the payout they receive in Montgomery Ward's reorganization.

"Because General Electric is both a significant lender to the company as well as a controlling shareholder, any action that takes place involving GE in the case will be examined closely by other creditors to be sure GE isn't using its influence inappropriately," said Joseph Julian, vice president with Houlihan Lokey Howard & Zukin, an investment bank.
GE controls five of the 10 board seats of the retailer's parent, Montgomery Ward Holding Corp., and owns its credit card business. GE recruited Chairman Roger Goddu from Toys "R" Us Inc. last year.
In addition, GE Capital has more than $900 million in unsecured claims against the company and agreed to lend Montgomery Ward $1 billion during the reorganization.

Conflicts of interest are not uncommon in bankruptcy cases. In R.H. Macy & Co. Inc.'s 1992 bankruptcy case, GE Capital had two seats on the retailer's board, managed its credit card business and was also a senior creditor.

During a court hearing this week in Wilmington, Del., GE Capital sought to allay concerns about its many roles in Montgomery Ward by saying a court decision in the Macy's case dealt with similar issues but found no conflict.

Montgomery Ward's lenders want to be sure the 408-store chain is not being unfairly charged by GE Capital for credit card services, thus decreasing the value of the company and the size of the pie available to creditors.
"The real issue making sure what GE does is not to the detriment of other creditors," said Henry Jackson, managing director of Peter J. Solomon Co., a New York investment bank.

GE Capital bought the credit card business from Montgomery Ward in 1988 during a buyout involving former Chairman Bernard Brennan. Analysts estimate GE Capital earns about $100 million a year from the Montgomery Ward credit card business.

During a court hearing in Wilmington on Tuesday, Montgomery Ward noted 50 percent of its sales are made with the private-label Monogram credit card, and it cannot afford an interruption in the business.

Montgomery Ward's lenders, including banks and insurance companies, objected to the company's effort to keep in place the agreements because they want to be sure GE has not worked out a "sweetheart" deal for servicing Monogram credit card receivables.
A GE Capital spokesman declined to comment on terms of those agreements.

But during the court hearing, the company noted the service pacts were in place when it bought Montgomery Ward's credit card business. In addition, the five non-GE Capital directors on Montgomery Ward's board approved the interim continuation of the agreements in a special vote, lawyers said during the hearing.
In addition to questioning the credit card agreements, lenders also asked whether Montgomery Ward was aggressive enough in seeking sources for the $1 billion in new financing.

The retailer said GE Capital's financing terms were better than those proposed by another lender that it did not disclose. Also, GE Capital noted other lenders were not stepping forward to extend Montgomery Ward fresh funds.

U.S. Bankruptcy Judge Peter Walsh ruled the credit card agreements should remain intact until a hearing July 31. Meanwhile, Montgomery Ward will provide information to other creditors to show that financial terms in its agreements with GE Capital were the best available.

"GE has been involved in a number of bankruptcy cases and restructuring, and they understand as well as anybody what you can and cannot do in accordance with the bankruptcy code," said Julian of Houlihan Lokey Howard & Zukin.
